resources.string: Ongoing control for the phonectl automation surface
Automation surface running. Tap Stop to halt all actions.
All automation is blocked. Tap Resume to allow actions again.
Read text from screenshot files (on-device OCR)
Read text from the current screen without saving screenshots
Granted — phonectl can read, reply to, and dismiss notifications. Tap to review.
Not granted. Tap to open Settings → Notifications → Device & app notifications → phonectl companion → Allow.
Set this as companion_token in phonectl config, then set companion_port. Loopback is not a security boundary on Android — this shared secret is what keeps other apps out. Tap to copy.
Stopped — all automation blocked. Tap to resume.
Active — automation allowed. Tap to stop.
The on-screen UI tree (element text, resource IDs, bounds, clickability). Passwords are never read from password fields.
Touch gestures and text insertion — only on behalf of phonectl CLI/MCP commands, never autonomously.
Notifications read: title, text, and action labels of active notifications; replies are sent only on behalf of phonectl commands.
OCR reads text from a screenshot you captured; images never leave the device (on-device ML-Kit). Used only as a fallback when the Tesseract binary is not installed.

The transport server binds 127.0.0.1 only, so no data leaves the device over the network. Loopback is NOT an app boundary on Android, so every request must also carry the pairing token — see the Pairing section.
Every action is logged to ~/.config/phonectl/actions.jsonl on the Python side. You can read this log at any time.
Password fields and payment screens are flagged so the phonectl policy layer can deny or confirm-gate actions. Guarded apps refuse gestures entirely.
